title: Dr. Seuss: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Dr. Seuss (Theodore Seuss Geisel), covering his Springfield, Massachusetts childhood and family brewery, pen name Theo LeSieg, Dartmouth and Jack O'Lantern humor magazine, early ad work for Flit and the fake Sious Navy for Standard Oil, WWII service at Fort Fox and the Battle of the Bulge, PM magazine cartooning, the wartime documentaries, the rhythm of a ship engine that inspired his anapestic tetrameter, And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street, Why Can't Johnny Read and the Cat in the Hat and Green Eggs and Ham, his wife Helen Palmer Geisel, his later progressive themes, the criticism of his early racist cartoons and the debate over his books in schools, Oh the Places You'll Go, and assorted trivia. The episode closes with year-end thanks and no listener mail.
topics: And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street

entities.name: And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street

segments.title: Opening banter and pronunciation of Seuss
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode, joke about the year's final show, and discuss the correct pronunciation of Seuss (Sois) and the Joe Theismann spelling story.

segments.title: Family brewery and childhood in Springfield
segments.summary: The Geisel family ran the Springfield Brewery, later shut down by Prohibition. Ted's father became superintendent of parks; the hosts debunk a myth about zoo drawings.

segments.title: Anti-German sentiment, pen name and Dartmouth
segments.summary: Geisel faced anti-German sentiment during World War I, began publishing under the pen name Theo LeSieg, and wrote for the Jack O'Lantern at Dartmouth until he was caught drinking during Prohibition.

segments.title: Oxford, Helen Palmer and the doctorate
segments.summary: Geisel went to Oxford, met his first wife Helen Palmer, who encouraged him toward art. He began working at Judge and adopted the Dr. title, later receiving an honorary Dartmouth degree.

segments.title: Break and listener shout-out
segments.summary: Break, with a shout-out to Mark Ruffalo for tweeting about the Navajo Code Talkers episode.

segments.title: Advertising career: Flit and the Sious Navy
segments.summary: Geisel became a nationally known ad illustrator, famous for Flit bug spray ads and the Quick, Henry, the Flit catchphrase, and then for the fictional Sious Navy promoting Standard Oil's marine oil.

segments.title: World War II, Fort Fox and the Battle of the Bulge
segments.summary: Geisel volunteered but was sent to Fort Fox in Hollywood, making training films. During a trip to Europe he was caught behind enemy lines for three days during the Battle of the Bulge.

segments.title: PM magazine and wartime documentaries
segments.summary: Geisel drew anti-fascist editorial cartoons for PM and made documentaries such as Your Job in Germany and Our Job in Japan, which MacArthur stopped and which were later recut.

segments.title: Children's books begin and anapestic meter
segments.summary: The rhythm of a transatlantic ship engine inspired his anapestic tetrameter. And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street, from a chance meeting with a Vanguard Press editor, launched his children's book career.
topics: And to Think That I Saw It on Mulberry Street

segments.title: Why Can't Johnny Read, Cat in the Hat and Green Eggs and Ham
segments.summary: Rudolf Flesch's book on reading instruction led to The Cat in the Hat as a reading primer. An editor's bet produced Green Eggs and Ham with fifty words. How the Grinch Stole Christmas followed the same year.

segments.title: Helen Palmer Geisel, Audrey Diamond and family life
segments.summary: Helen Palmer Geisel was an author who managed business affairs and died by suicide in 1967 after decades of marriage; Geisel then married Audrey Diamond. The hosts discuss his not wanting children.

segments.title: Early racist cartoons and the modern debate
segments.summary: Geisel's early college, magazine and ad work included racist and anti-Japanese caricatures. The hosts discuss his later progressive books, the Read Across America controversy, and a librarian's rejection of a gift of his books.

segments.title: Oh, the Places You'll Go and final trivia
segments.summary: Oh, the Places You'll Go was his last book published in his lifetime and his best-seller, popular with graduates. Trivia follows about his chain smoking and corn cob pipe, and a federal judge's egg poem.

segments.title: Year-end sign-off
segments.summary: No listener mail this week; the hosts thank listeners for the year and wish a happy birthday to Chuck's wife.
